**Explanation:**
The story makes sophisticated use of extended metaphor and surreal imagery to convey deeper thematic insights about obsolescence, grief, and clinging to the past. 

Rather than relying on standard figurative expressions, the writer constructs a powerful structural metaphor in which the woman is a literal and figurative counterpart to the discarded armchair on the curb. Both the chair and the woman feature a pattern of yellow flowers on green stems, and both have a blackened, burned left arm. While the narrator has become professionally obsolete—continuing to "inventory" the world after his job has disappeared—the woman and the chair represent physical and domestic obsolescence or trauma. 

Furthermore, the narrator neatly encapsulates his own psychological state through metaphor and simile, noting that the city puts out furniture "as though a flood were an inspection for which one could prepare," and describing his lingering habit of observation as "an intention no longer attached to a task." When the narrator finally takes a piece of the ruined chair's fabric and folds it into his pocket, the metaphor culminates in a poignant act of preservation, showing his desire to hold onto and catalog what the rest of the world has deemed ruined or unwanted.
